newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech trade data disappoints but crown indifferent.
newsitem.headline: Czech trade data disappoints but crown indifferent.

text.p: Czech April trade figures released on Monday were worse than expected, but analysts said it was too early to say whether a recent positive trend had come to an end, while the besieged crown reacted indifferently.

Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said on May 19 that preliminary figures showed the trade deficit for April, boosted by strong export growth of some 26 percent, year-on-year, would ease to about 11.4 billion crowns.
But official preliminary data released by the Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) on Monday showed an April shortfall of 15.34 billion crowns, up from a revised 13.08 billion in March.

"The figures are not what we had hoped, but it is hard to say if this is the end of the positive trend or just a bump in the road. At this point, we aren't changing our outlook," said Boris Gomez of ING Barings in Prague.
Petr Kukla of Girocredit said: "For the Prime Minister, this is kind of a shame. He said 11.4 billion crowns but the final figures are actually much higher."

The CSU said in a statement that imports for the first four months of 1997 rose by 11.2 percent, year-on-year, to 261.7 billion crowns, while imports edged up an annual 6.3 percent to 208 billion crowns.

It added that fossil fuels, foodstuffs and industrial goods were at the heart of the rise in imports, while exports were spurred mainly through machinery, which recorded a year-on-year increase of 19.4 percent.

Analysts said that the positive development of rising exports continued in April, posting their highest growth rate this year, but added that after three months of stable import growth, April showed a marked, and troubling, increase.

"It's hard to tell what the reason for the increase in imports was, but keeping in mind that last year we saw the widening deficit trend take off in April, this could be a bad sign," said one London-based economist.
ING's Gomez said the rise in imports may be attributed to firms trying to beat the imposition of the government's import deposit plan near the end of April.
Under the deposit plan, importers of consumer and agricultural goods must deposit sums equal to 20 percent of the value of their imports in non-interest bearing accounts at Czech banks for 180 days.
"There were rumours leading up to the actual announcement of the plan that something would happen, and some firms may have loaded up on goods before its imposition," he said.

The import restrictions were part of a sweeping package of measures announced by the government last week to boost growth, reform the capital markets and generally restore faith in the country's commitment to radical economic reform.

"The export growth may suggest that some of the machinery and industrial imports over the past two years are finally translating through, but again it's too early to tell, it could just be gains off of the weaker crown," Gomez added.
The crown has been under heavy downward pressure as the trade gap has caused an already large current account deficit to grow to more than nine percent of gross domestic product.
But the crown, which hit a record low against its dollar/mark basket midpoint of -6.4 percent last week, reacted indifferently to the data.

"The figures were disappointing, but there are so few crowns left in the market that we saw little effect," said one forex trader, adding that activity was slower than usual due to holidays in London and New York.
The crown was trading at around -3.0 percent against basket parity just after the figures were released, and was later fixed by the central bank at -2.80 percent.

Recently, the central bank has been holding several repo tenders daily in order to drain liquidity from the market and help the support the crown from a wave of short-selling by speculative foreign investors.
The CNB also cut off banks' access to the Lombard credit, and limited non-residents' participation on the local money market last week to boost the crown.
